# Measure retrieval bloat before/after 4.0: recorded transcript bytes vs replayed bytes in replay-queries, and a live per-call size metric

## Why
4.0.0 shipped the retrieval bloat fixes (#170 sanitize, #171 search caps, #172 hook injection cap) and the unified entries model (#176). Before releasing 4.0.1 or flipping the default (#192) the owner wants evidence that the token burn actually dropped, not a parity score. The replay harness (#182) measures agreement between read paths; it does not measure size, and nothing on the server records how many bytes each tool call returns.

## Raw material
The Claude Code session transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/*.jsonl hold every mcm tool_use together with the tool_result the client actually received from the basement (3.16.x until 2026-10-21). First pass over all transcripts, bytes of `search` results by day, pre-fix:

```
day         n   total     median   p90     max
2026-09-07  41  336 KB    6479     16333   46062
2026-09-14  46  461 KB    10176    16136   23547
2026-10-02  79  708 KB    6114     20023   48166  (3 persisted as "Output too large")
2026-10-11  88  686 KB    4634     21263   30092
2026-10-14  28  427 KB    15864    31230   45529
```
Typical day: 300 to 700 KB of search output, median 5 to 10 KB per call, p90 15 to 25 KB, max around 45 KB.

## Build
1. `extract_queries` also captures the recorded result bytes by pairing each tool_use id with its tool_result.
2. `replay` records `recorded_bytes`, `legacy_bytes`, `unified_bytes` per query and aggregates per tool: total, median, p90, and the ratio replayed/recorded. Printed by `format_report`, written to the JSON.
3. Run on the mcm_rehearsal Postgres in natural mode (what the basement runs) and on the SQLite snapshot; store the numbers in the KB.
4. Live metric going forward: record response bytes per tool call on the server so the same statistic can be read from the basement after the fact, not only from client transcripts. Scope to be decided in this issue after the replay numbers are in; `session_metrics` may be the right home.

## Acceptance
- `mcm-engine replay-queries <transcripts> --store <dsn> --query-mode natural` prints, per tool, recorded vs replayed byte totals, medians and p90s.
- Harness test: a fixture whose tool_results have known lengths yields the expected recorded bytes, and a replayed result of a known length yields the expected ratio.
- The before/after numbers for `search` and `report_error` are stored in the KB with the corpus drift stated (snapshot 2026-10-20 vs transcript dates).

# Cap retrieval output in summary search: inline Why/Fix length, hit budget, common-token downrank

`search` summary mode is small for KNOWLEDGE/RULE but still bloats on NEGATIVE/ERROR and on low-value matches. A sohot session's `search("sweep-check")` and `search("deploy guard")` each returned ~20 hits, including the same 6-7 irrelevant NEGATIVEs (#1,#3,#8,#10,#11,#14,#16) matched only on a common token ("check"/"sweep"/"deploy"/"testing"), each inlining its full (and currently polluted) Why/Fix. Even post-sanitize (#170) the Why/Fix is multi-paragraph; a one-line hit is cheap, seven 2 KB inlined bodies are not.

## Fix (search.py)
1. Cap the inline NEGATIVE Why/Fix and ERROR root_cause/fix in summary mode at a few hundred chars each, with a "… (get_entry for full)" pointer. `detail="full"` stays uncapped.
2. Cap total hits returned per query. The public `search` default `limit` is 10 per entity type → up to 40 + related. Add an overall response ceiling (~8-10 hits) independent of per-scope limit.
3. Downrank or drop a hit whose only match is a single common token: when a NEGATIVE/ERROR matches on a token that is also a stopword-ish high-frequency term and nothing more distinctive, it should not outrank or crowd out a real RULE hit. Simplest: a relevance floor for NEGATIVE/ERROR in the multi-scope "all" path so generic single-token matches drop below the fold.

## Acceptance
- `search("deploy guard")` and `search("sweep-check")` each return under ~3 KB, with RULE #756 and #868 still present for "deploy guard".
- `detail="full"` is unchanged (still returns whole bodies).

# Sanitize NEGATIVE/ERROR serialized-blob pollution + store-time guard (#142 follow-on)

Follow-on to #142 (closed), which cleaned only the KNOWLEDGE table (94/516 summaries re-split). The same serialized-entry leak exists in the NEGATIVE and ERROR tables and was never covered: `sanitize_knowledge` iterates `EntityType.KNOWLEDGE` only, and `clean_summary_detail` is summary/detail-specific, so it cannot repair the NEGATIVE three-field (`what_failed`/`why_failed`/`correct_approach`) or ERROR (`pattern`/`context`/`root_cause`/`fix`) shape.

## Evidence (live basement, 3.16.0)
`get_entry('negative', 10|11|16)` show the entire XML-serialized entry crammed into `what_failed`: the real text, then `</what_failed>`, then `<parameter name="why_failed">…</parameter>`, `<parameter name="correct_approach">…`, `<parameter name="project">…`, `<parameter name="tags">…`, `</invoke>`. The real `why_failed`/`correct_approach` columns are empty. ~2 KB each. #3 and #6 are variants. Because #136 keeps NEGATIVE Why/Fix inline in summary search, every hit on one of these ships the whole blob.

## Fix
1. Add `clean_negative(what_failed, why_failed, correct_approach)` and `clean_error(pattern, context, root_cause, fix)` to `sanitize.py`: when the headline field carries the serialized blob, parse out each `<parameter name="FIELD">…</parameter>` into its proper column, keep the clean prefix before the first marker as the headline, and strip `project`/`tags`/`</invoke>` tails. Reuse the existing marker regexes.
2. Extend the corpus tool to sweep all three tables. Either generalize `sanitize_knowledge` to a `sanitize_corpus(entity_type="all")` or add NEGATIVE/ERROR passes; keep `dry_run` default True.
3. Store-time guard: in `add_negative` / `report_error` (and `add_knowledge`), run the field through the cleaner on write so a new serialized blob can never re-enter. Deterministic, fail-open, no reject — split silently and store clean.

## Acceptance
- A dry-run reports the polluted NEGATIVE/ERROR ids (incl. #3,#6,#10,#11,#16); apply re-splits them into clean columns with no data loss (salvaged text lands in the right field).
- A fresh `add_negative` whose field contains a `</invoke>`/`<parameter>` fragment stores clean columns.
- Re-scan reports 0 polluted across knowledge+negative+error.

# #137e: replay evaluation harness + evidence-based retune (absorbs #149)

Child of #137. **Absorbs the remaining work of #149** (evidence-based retune of guessed constants).

Build a replay harness over the historical tool-call workload to evaluate candidate retrieval-trigger policies, reporting the two error rates **weighted asymmetrically**:
- **False negative** (a lookup should have happened, policy skipped it) — weighted *much* heavier, especially when the missed memory is a prior observed failure or an explicit user constraint.
- **False positive** (a lookup enforced when nothing relevant existed).

Honest limitation to state up front: replay evaluates *trigger* decisions but cannot predict how Claude behaves *after* receiving different memory — that needs **live paired task evaluations**. Include a plan for those.

Then feed the #149 knobs (scoring weights `W_*`, dedup thresholds, search `RANK_THRESHOLD`/`STALE_DAYS`, rulesift thresholds — all already env-overridable via `tunables.py` from PR #151) into this harness and retune with evidence instead of guessing. Each retune is its own PR with its evidence.

### Acceptance
- Replay harness reporting FN/FP rates (FN weighted) for candidate policies.
- A written plan for live paired eval.
- At least the ranking weights + search thresholds swept and retuned (or explicitly confirmed) with harness evidence.

# #137b: UserPromptSubmit task-aware retrieval + inject

Child of #137. **Highest implement-today leverage.**

Add a `UserPromptSubmit` hook: classify each new request; when it references historical decisions, prior failures, established preferences, or ongoing work, search automatically and inject the result via `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` *before* the model reasons. Establishes coverage (updates the #137 ledger) without the agent initiating a tool call.

Note: this hook blocks prompt processing until it returns — keep it fast. Classification deterministic-first (keyword/pattern), LLM only at the ambiguous+consequential margin (mcm runs model-agnostic behind a LiteLLM gateway per DECISION #39 — an LLM-evaluated hook is a gateway round-trip on the critical path). Fail-open on infra failure (RULE #61).

### Acceptance
- `mcm-engine` exposes a UserPromptSubmit handler wired in settings.
- History-referencing prompts auto-retrieve + inject via additionalContext; non-historical prompts do nothing (fast path).
- Retrieval updates the coverage ledger.
- Tests for the classifier (deterministic cases) + injection shape.

# #137a: server-owned per-session topic-coverage ledger + compaction reconciliation

Child of #137 (retrieval scheduling umbrella). **The foundation — the other layers depend on this.**

Give mcm-engine a lightweight **server-owned, per-FastMCP-session** retrieval ledger: coverage by *topic* (not TTL), each entry carrying `{topic, searched_at, query, result_ids, resident}`. Only the server sees the query + result ids, so the server owns it; the PreToolUse hook (a separate process) reads shared state or asks the server.

Critical requirement — **coverage is not context residency** (KB CONTEXT #3, the founding anti-amnesia concern): a ledger that says "topic covered" after the retrieved bodies were summarized out of context recreates the exact failure mcm-engine exists to defeat. So carry a `resident` flag distinct from `searched_at`, and **reconcile it at the compaction boundary** — on `PreCompact`/`PostCompact` and `SessionStart`, mark prior coverage non-resident (or re-surface it). A non-resident topic does not satisfy enforcement.

Keyed per FastMCP session (RULE #116 / ScopedTracker), same as the existing tracker state.

### Acceptance
- Server-owned, per-session, per-topic coverage ledger with a `resident` flag.
- `search` (and report_error auto-search) record coverage: topic, query, result_ids, searched_at, resident=true.
- Reconciled at PreCompact/PostCompact/SessionStart (resident flips false on compaction).
- Unit tests for record + reconcile; no behavior change to enforcement yet (that's the PreToolUse child).

# KB data pollution: some knowledge summaries contain the whole serialized body (incl. a leaked </invoke> fragment)

## Observed
Under 3.12.0 summary-mode `search`, a subset of KNOWLEDGE hits render with stray structural markup — `</summary>`, `<detail>…</detail>`, `<rationale>`, `<references>`, `<tags>`, `<kind>`, `<project>`, and a trailing `</invoke>`.

## Root cause (verified via get_entry)
Not a formatter bug. `get_entry("knowledge", 157)` shows the stored **`summary` column** itself contains the entire XML-serialized entry, e.g.:

```
summary: Measured 2026-09-20 … permanently inert.</summary>
<detail>…</detail>
<rationale>…</rationale>
<tags>…</tags>
<kind>finding</kind>
<project>localharness</project>
</invoke>
```

The renderer prints stored fields faithfully; clean entries (all rules, recent knowledge) render clean. So a batch of entries was created with a pre-serialized blob passed as the `summary`/content, and a tool-call fragment (`</invoke>`) was captured at store time.

## Scope
Appears concentrated in imported `localharness`/`sohot` findings. Exact count TBD as part of the fix (FTS can't easily match raw tags; needs a direct scan of `knowledge.summary` for `</invoke>` / `</detail>` / `</summary>`).

## Impact
Cosmetic + token waste: polluted summaries defeat the #119 progressive-disclosure saving (the whole body ships in the "summary"). No correctness impact on search/ranking.

## Fix (two parts, both non-blocking for the next release)
1. **Data cleanup**: scan `knowledge.summary` for embedded field tags; for each, re-split into clean `summary` + `detail` and update in place (DB is authoritative — update via the MCP, no file writes).
2. **Prevention (optional, code)**: `add_knowledge`/`add_rule` could reject or strip content containing tool-call fragments or mismatched field tags, so a malformed store can't recur.

Found 2026-10-14 while characterizing 3.12.0 MCP behavior post-deploy.

# Audit guessed hardcoded constants: provenance, env-override, and evidence-based retune

## Thesis
The hook thresholds (`WARN_THRESHOLD`, `BLOCK_THRESHOLD`) were acknowledged by the owner as numbers guessed with no backing evidence, which happened not to need changing until #144/#146. They are almost certainly not the only ones. The codebase carries many module-level numeric constants that shape behavior — scoring weights, similarity thresholds, decay windows — and the KB already records, repeatedly, that invented thresholds mislead (FINDING #163 "any threshold chosen now is invented"; RULE #303 "measuring a configuration nobody runs"; FINDING #5 dedup-threshold false positives).

This issue is the durable inventory + a triage, not a one-time list in a chat.

## The inventory command (re-run any time)
```
grep -rnE '^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]+ *= *-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?\b' src/mcm_engine/ | grep -vE '/__pycache__/'
```
40 hits today. (It over-captures: default-kwarg magic numbers and in-function literals are not caught, and structural constants are. Triage separates them.)

## Triage
**Behavior-shaping knobs — need a measured justification in the KB, or an explicit "guessed, unvalidated" acknowledgment, and ideally env-overridable:**
- `scoring.py`: W_RELEVANCE 2.0, W_HIT 0.1, W_REINFORCEMENT 0.3, W_CORRECTNESS 0.5, W_RECENCY 0.3, W_IMPORTANCE 0.5, W_SCOPE 0.1, PINNED_WEIGHT 2.0, HIT_SATURATION 10.0, REINFORCEMENT_SATURATION 3.0, CORRECTNESS_SCALE 2.0, RECENCY_WINDOW_DAYS 30.0, RECENCY_MAX_BONUS 1.0 — the entire ranking formula is hand-weighted.
- `dedup.py`: TOPIC_THRESHOLD 0.5, BODY_THRESHOLD 0.4, SUBSUME_THRESHOLD 0.8, MIN_ENTROPY 1.5 — FINDING #5 already measured these produce false positives / miss semantic conflicts.
- `tools/search.py`: RANK_THRESHOLD 1.0, STALE_DAYS 90, EXPIRED_PENALTY 0.1.
- `ingest/rulesift.py`: KNOWN_THRESHOLD 0.9, NOVEL_THRESHOLD 0.5, MIN_TOKENS 3, MIN_SUBSTANCE_TOKENS 6.
- `hooks/mcp_enforcement.py`: WARN_THRESHOLD 8, BLOCK_THRESHOLD 20, FIXATION_THRESHOLD 8, AMBIENT_MAX_PER_SESSION 8 (the originating case; retune belongs with #137's coverage evidence).
- `destructive.py`: DEFAULT_ARCHIVE_FLOOR 5, DEFAULT_ARCHIVE_FRACTION 0.5.

# search summary mode should carry a match snippet (keep 'why it matched' under semantic/non-FTS5 backends)

## Problem

#119 made `search` default to compact summary hits (id, kind, title/topic, one-line summary, tags) and defer bodies to `get_entry`. That progressive-disclosure win rests on an implicit assumption: the agent can judge a hit's relevance *from the summary line* and only fetch the bodies worth paying for.

That assumption holds under **lexical** search (SQLite FTS5, Postgres FTS), where the query token is literally in the matched text, so the agent knows why a hit came back. It weakens under a **semantic/vector** backend (the direction the live server + lodestone are moving — FTS5 is being retired): a hit can match on meaning the summary line never surfaces, so the agent can't tell from the one-liner whether the body is relevant. Result: either wasted `get_entry` round-trips on bad hits, or wrongly skipping a good hit. No wrong results, but the ergonomics of summary-first degrade exactly where we're headed.

## Root cause

`detail`/summary rendering (`tools/search.py`) is fully decoupled from the search backend (good — see `_scope_block`), but `SearchHit` (`backends/__init__.py:323`) carries `entity_type / entity_id / score / is_pinned / is_stale / counters_snapshot / row` and **no matched-text field**. The "why it matched" signal every backend computes internally is thrown away before rendering.

## Proposal

Add an optional `snippet: Optional[str] = None` to `SearchHit`. Each adapter populates it from the highlight it already produces; summary-mode rendering appends it under the one-liner when present. Adapters that can't produce one leave it `None` and rendering falls back to today's behavior — no regression, no required work for any adapter.

Per-adapter source of the snippet:
- **SQLite FTS5**: `snippet()` / `highlight()` aux functions.
- **Postgres**: `ts_headline()` over the indexed document.
- **OpenSearch**: the `highlight` block already in the response.
- **Semantic/vector backend (future)**: the matched chunk/passage it ranked on — this is the case the issue exists for.

Summary rendering: append a short, length-capped snippet line to each hit in `detail="summary"`. `detail="full"` is unchanged (it already has the whole body). Keep the once-per-response `get_entry` footer.

## Acceptance
- `SearchHit.snippet` optional, defaults `None`; omitting it is valid for any adapter.
- At least the lexical adapters (SQLite, Postgres) populate it; summary hits render it when present.
- Snippet length is bounded (config, e.g. `MCM_SNIPPET_MAX`) so this doesn't reintroduce the token bloat #119 removed.
- Conformance covers: snippet present renders; snippet `None` renders exactly as today.

## Non-goals
- Not changing matching, ranking, or `include_archived`.
- Not changing the summary-vs-full default.
- Not building the semantic backend here — only making sure summary mode can carry its match signal when it lands.

Follow-up to #119.

# search summary mode must keep Why/Fix inline for NEGATIVE (and ERROR) hits

## Problem

#119 strips the body from a hit in `detail="summary"` (the default). For ordinary knowledge that only makes a hit *incomplete* — worst case you `get_entry` it. For **negative knowledge** it is a correctness bug, because the body **is** the payload and the failure mode is asymmetric.

`tools/search.py:272` renders a NEGATIVE summary hit as just:

    [NEGATIVE #id] <category>: <what_failed>

`Why` (`why_failed`) and `Fix` (`correct_approach`) are gated behind `detail == "full"` (lines 273-277). So a plain `search` tells the agent *that* an approach failed but hides *why it must stay rejected* and *what to do instead*. The agent can then re-attempt the dead end, or be unable to tell whether its current plan is the rejected one — the exact outcome the anti-pattern store exists to prevent. ERROR hits have the same shape: `root_cause` / `fix` are gated at `tools/search.py:296`.

Note #122 only restored full bodies for the `report_error` auto-search path. A direct `search(scope="negative")` (or an all-scope search that surfaces a negative) still strips Why/Fix.

## Why this is the right asymmetry

The #119 token win comes from not carrying large *knowledge* bodies. Negative/error bodies are short (a Why line + a Fix line), so keeping them inline barely dents the win, and their whole value is being seen at the moment of the hit, not one `get_entry` later.

## Proposal

In summary mode, keep `Why`/`Fix` inline for NEGATIVE hits and `root_cause`/`fix` for ERROR hits. Knowledge stays summary-only (its bodies are the token problem). Optionally cap each field's length (reuse whatever `MCM_SNIPPET_MAX`-style bound #135 lands) so a pathologically long negative can't reintroduce bloat.

## Acceptance
- `search` (summary, default) renders Why + Fix for a NEGATIVE hit and root cause + fix for an ERROR hit.
- Knowledge summary rendering unchanged.
- Conformance: a negative/error hit in summary mode contains its Why/Fix (root cause/fix); a knowledge hit in summary mode still omits its body.

Follow-up to #119 / #122. Distinct from #135 (which adds a match *snippet*); this is about which structured fields summary mode keeps per kind.

# export --remote: write the KB to .md files over MCP (no pod exec, no direct DB)

## Problem

`mcm-engine export-mirror --from <DSN> --out <DIR>` renders active rules to `rules/<category>/<slug>.md` and commits them — but `--from` is a **DSN**: it connects directly to the store. For the real deployment (KB in a remote pod, client on a laptop) that means either pointing at the remote Postgres directly (breaks "the interface is the MCP call, never touch the remote DB directly") or `kubectl exec` / a Job inside the pod and copying the tree down. Running export from inside the pod is a non-starter operationally.

There is no MCP-native export today. This is the **export twin of `ingest --remote`** (#72/#73): the same co-location gap, the other direction (KB → files).

## Design: the symmetric split

Data flows KB → client (bulk read of full rule bodies). Rendering `.md` is client-side; reading the corpus is a server MCP call.

- **Server (new MCP tool `export_rules`):** returns a **page** of active rules with full content — `[{id, title, keywords, category, content, status}, ...]` — via `offset`/`limit`, bounded by a per-call cap (like `MCM_SIFT_MAX_SPANS` in #76). Skips archived/superseded, mirroring `export_mirror`. Rules only (matches export-mirror's scope).
- **Client (`mcm-engine export-mirror --remote --out DIR`):** pages through `export_rules` over MCP, then writes the tree client-side reusing the existing mirror rendering (`_generate_rule_content`, `_slugify`, `rules/<category>/<slug>.md`, slug-collision suffixes). Git commit optional (`--no-commit`), since a fresh client env may lack a git identity — the operational gotcha in the direct path.

## Scope (one PR, TDD)

1. **Factor the renderer.** Extract `mirror.render_rules_to_tree(rows, out_dir)` (write `rules/<category>/<slug>.md` + collision handling) so both the direct `export_mirror` and the remote client share one code path. `export_mirror` keeps its git-commit behavior on top.
2. **`export_rules` MCP tool** (in `register_rules_tools`): `export_rules(offset=0, limit=100)` → structured page of active rules with content; caps `limit` at `MCM_EXPORT_PAGE_MAX` (default e.g. 200); documents that total transfer scales O(rules) so clients must page. Read-only.
3. **`export-mirror --remote --out DIR`** client: resolve endpoint via `_mcp_http_endpoint` (auth from #74), page with the #75 resilience helpers (`_classify_remote_error`, retry-with-backoff on transient, per-page timeout), render each page to the tree, then optionally `git add -A` + commit. `--remote` is incompatible with `--from`.

## Reuse (already in the tree from remote-ingest)

- **Auth** (#74): `_mcp_http_endpoint` → headers from `.mcp.json` / `MCM_MCP_TOKEN`, threaded into `mcp_http_call_tool`.
- **Resilience** (#75): `_classify_remote_error`, retry/backoff, per-call timeout via `mcp_http_call_tool(timeout=…)`. Export is read-only + paged, so resume is optional (a re-run is cheap and idempotent — it rewrites the tree).
- **Per-call cap pattern** (#76): a page cap so one call can't outrun the transport.

## Non-goals (this issue)

- Server-side git commit (the client commits, optionally).
- Delta/incremental export — full dump for v1.
- Exporting knowledge / negatives / errors — rules only, matching `export-mirror`.

## Why it matters

Symmetric with `ingest --remote`: files stay local, corpus logic stays in the pod, everything crosses as an MCP call. Makes "dump the KB to a diffable `.md` tree" a first-class laptop operation against a hosted, auth-required KB — no pod exec, no direct Postgres.

## Related
- #72 / #73 — `ingest --remote` (the ingest half of this pattern)
- #74 — MCP auth headers (reused)
- #75 — client batching/retry/resume (reused)
- #76 — per-call cap pattern (reused)

# In-session style nudge: positive voice exemplar, not a longer denylist

## Problem

Stylistic tics (emojis, em-dashes, "it's not X, it's Y", rule-of-three cadence, "great question", empty intensifiers) leak back into responses over the course of a session, and get worse as context fills. Two mechanisms, and they need different fixes:

1. **Instruction decay.** The style rule lives in CLAUDE.md / MEMORY.md at the top of the window. As the session grows, generation happens further from that instruction and soft stylistic constraints slip first. Well-established behavior.
2. **Precedent accumulation.** The model conditions on the whole window. As tool output, git logs, PR bodies, and the mandated `Generated with Claude Code` trailer pile up, the local prior for "an emoji/tic is normal here" drifts up. Long sessions correlate with high context, but the causal driver is probably *what* accumulated, not raw token count.

A periodic MCP nudge addresses (1). It does little for (2).

## Why the current rule reads clinical

The existing guidance is a denylist: no em-dashes, no emojis, no LinkedIn-speak, no "it's not X, it's Y". Every clause is a prohibition. The safest way to satisfy an all-prohibition rule is to strip out all personality, because personality is where the risk lives. Flat, dry prose violates nothing. So the denylist doesn't just permit clinical, it pulls toward it.

Second problem: naming a tic primes the tic. A reminder that says "don't use emojis" puts emojis in the context. Negative instructions are weak in general and self-defeating here in particular.

## Proposed direction

**Give a positive voice target, phrased as an exemplar, not a longer denylist.** The warmth we want is not surface affect (enthusiasm, "happy to help", emoji). It's substance: read the actual situation, take a position, be brief, say the dry true thing when there is one. Directness and judgment read as warmth once the decorative warmth is gone.

**Store examples, not adjectives.** "Be warm, be direct" decays into clinical because adjectives are cheap to satisfy. Two or three before/after pairs give the model something to pattern-match, which is what it's actually good at. One paragraph in the target voice sitting in context beats a page of rules about the voice.

**Two layers, mirroring the project's own MCP-nudge + PreToolUse-hook split:**
- *Soft:* the voice is un-filterable, so it lives in the nudge as a positive exemplar, re-surfaced periodically to fight decay. Keep it terse; over-nudging produces self-conscious, trying-too-hard prose.
- *Hard:* the absolute bans (zero emojis, em-dash count) are mechanical. Put them in a post-filter or counter, not a polite reminder. You can't regex your way to "warm," but you can regex "no emoji", and the same counting yields a real metric instead of eyeballing leakage.

## Example before/after pairs

**A. Opener + rule-of-three + outro**

> Before: Great question! Let's dive into how the dispatcher works. At its core, the ingester registry is powerful, flexible, and easy to extend. By walking each ingester in order, we can seamlessly match the right one. I hope this helps clarify things!

> After: The registry walks each ingester in registration order and takes the first that matches. That order is the precedence: specific ingesters first, text-dir last. To add one, implement `matches` and `stream` and call `register`.

**B. "It's not X, it's Y" + em-dash + empty intensifiers**

> Before: This isn't just a bug fix, it's a fundamental rethink of how we handle net-new detection. The new approach is remarkably robust and leverages content hashing to deliver a truly seamless deduplication experience.

> After: The old title-only dedup missed the same rule pasted under a different title. Now we hash the content, so a duplicate body is caught no matter what it's called. Same idea, one more check at the write path.

**C. Hedging + restating the question + bullets-on-everything**

> Before: You asked whether the ingest is idempotent. That's a great thing to verify. It's worth noting that, generally speaking, the system is designed to be idempotent on topic and kind, safe to re-run, and resilient to duplicates. So in most cases, you should be fine re-running it.

> After: Yes. It dedups on (topic, kind) at the write path, so re-running updates in place instead of inserting again. Run it twice and the second pass is a no-op.

## Open questions to ruminate on

- Where does the exemplar live so it re-surfaces without burning tokens every turn? Pinned item, folded into the existing store-reminder nudge, or a dedicated low-frequency channel?
- Nudge cadence. Frequent enough to fight decay, sparse enough to avoid self-conscious prose. What interval?
- Does the soft exemplar survive compaction, or does it need to be re-anchored the way MEMORY.md is?
- Is the hard filter worth it, or does a counter/metric (count tells per response, surface a number) get most of the value without the risk of a filter mangling legitimate output?
- Whose calibration anchors "warm but not clinical"? The exemplar set is the calibration, so it needs curating, not just writing once.

Not for immediate build. Filed for rumination.

# get_last_session returns the global latest handoff — no per-caller/workspace scoping, so shared deployments resume the wrong session

## Summary

On any deployment where more than one working context shares a single mcm-engine store (multiple users behind one server, or one user across several projects), `session_start` and `get_resume_context` routinely surface a handoff belonging to a *different* context. The user asks to resume project A and is handed project B's handoff.

## Root cause

`get_last_session` is unscoped in both adapters:

```python
# adapters/sqlite/storage.py
"SELECT * FROM sessions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
# adapters/postgres/storage.py — identical
```

It returns the single newest row across the entire `sessions` table. There is only ever one candidate, so "resume" can't pick correctly — it picks globally-latest.

Contributing facts:
- The `sessions` table (`schema.py`) has **no scoping column** — no project, no owner/principal — unlike `knowledge`/`negative_knowledge`/`errors`, which all carry `project` (and project indexes).
- `session_handoff` accepts only `status/current_task/next_steps/blockers` — the client cannot tag a handoff with any scope key at write time.
- `get_last_session(*, caller=None)` already has a **vestigial `caller` param that is never populated or used** for filtering.
- Both `session_start` (the "Last handoff" block) and `get_resume_context` call `get_last_session()` with no argument.

## Why `project_name` alone doesn't fix it

`MCM_PROJECT_NAME` is a **server-global** config value — every request through one server carries the same project. Adding a `project` column keyed to `MCM_PROJECT_NAME` would sort every caller into the same bucket and change nothing for the common "one shared server" topology. It also wouldn't separate a single user's multiple projects.

The scoping key has to be **per-request**, not per-server.

## What's already available

`principal.py` exposes `get_transport_principal()` — the bearer-token identity for the in-flight request, carried in a ContextVar and already used as the fallback in `resolve_actor()`. So an authenticated per-caller identity is reachable from any tool call today; the session tools simply don't consult it.

## Proposed fix

1. **Schema:** add scoping columns to `sessions` — at minimum `principal TEXT` (who), and an optional client-supplied `workspace TEXT` label (what — so one principal working on N projects stays separated). Additive migration + index, mirroring the `project` columns on the other tables.
2. **Write:** `session_handoff` stamps the current transport principal automatically, and accepts an optional `workspace` argument (or derives one — see open question) so the row is self-describing.
3. **Read:** `get_last_session(*, principal=None, workspace=None)` → `WHERE` on the provided keys, `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`. `session_start` / `get_resume_context` pass the in-flight principal (+ workspace when known).
4. **Back-compat:** pre-migration rows have NULL scope. Treat a NULL-scope handoff as a **clearly-labeled global fallback**, shown only when no scoped row matches, so existing handoffs aren't orphaned.

## Open question for maintainer

What should `workspace` derive from when the client doesn't pass one? Options: (a) principal-only scoping (simplest, but conflates one user's multiple projects); (b) an explicit client-supplied label on `session_handoff`/`session_start`; (c) something the client already sends (e.g. a cwd/repo hint). Leaning (b) with (a) as the fallback, but the right default depends on how you want stdio/unauthenticated contexts (principal = None) to behave — today they'd all collapse to the NULL bucket.

## Impact

Silent and confusing: the agent confidently narrates the wrong project's state as if it were the current one, and a user who trusts it can act on stale/irrelevant context. Severity scales with the number of concurrent contexts sharing the store.

```python
"SELECT * FROM sessions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
# adapters/postgres/storage.py — identical
```

It returns the single newest row across the entire `sessions` table. There is only ever one candidate, so "resume" can't pick correctly — it picks globally-latest.

Contributing facts:
- The `sessions` table (`schema.py`) has **no scoping column** — no project, no owner/principal — unlike `knowledge`/`negative_knowledge`/`errors`, which all carry `project` (and project indexes).
- `session_handoff` accepts only `status/current_task/next_steps/blockers` — the client cannot tag a handoff with any scope key at write time.
- `get_last_session(*, caller=None)` already has a **vestigial `caller` param that is never populated or used** for filtering.
- Both `session_start` (the "Last handoff" block) and `get_resume_context` call `get_last_session()` with no argument.

## Why `project_name` alone doesn't fix it

`MCM_PROJECT_NAME` is a **server-global** config value — every request through one server carries the same project. Adding a `project` column keyed to `MCM_PROJECT_NAME` would sort every caller into the same bucket and change nothing for the common "one shared server" topology. It also wouldn't separate a single user's multiple projects.

The scoping key has to be **per-request**, not per-server.

## What's already available

`principal.py` exposes `get_transport_principal()` — the bearer-token identity for the in-flight request, carried in a ContextVar and already used as the fallback in `resolve_actor()`. So an authenticated per-caller identity is reachable from any tool call today; the session tools simply don't consult it.

## Open question for maintainer

What should `workspace` derive from when the client doesn't pass one? Options: (a) principal-only scoping (simplest, but conflates one user's multiple projects); (b) an explicit client-supplied label on `session_handoff`/`session_start`; (c) something the client already sends (e.g. a cwd/repo hint). Leaning (b) with (a) as the fallback, but the right default depends on how you want stdio/unauthenticated contexts (principal = None) to behave — today they'd all collapse to the NULL bucket.

## Impact

Silent and confusing: the agent confidently narrates the wrong project's state as if it were the current one, and a user who trusts it can act on stale/irrelevant context. Severity scales with the number of concurrent contexts sharing the store.

# stdio startup sync failure is invisible to the client: server reports ready and serves a stale index

In stdio mode, a failed startup sync is invisible to the client. The server comes up, reports ready, and serves a stale index — searches then return confident "no results" for rules that exist on disk and are committed.

`server.py` `run()` catches it and moves on:

```python
try:
    counts = self.watcher.sync_once()
    log(f"sync_rules at stdio startup: {counts}")
except Exception as e:
    log(f"sync_rules at stdio startup failed (non-fatal): {e}")
self.mcp.run()
```

The log line is real and lands in `log_path`, but `log()` writes to file only and deliberately never touches stderr ("MCP clients treat stderr as failure"). Nothing reaches the client, and no tool response carries a staleness signal, so neither the agent nor the user has any way to learn the index is behind the files.

Observed twice on a single-user laptop, 2026-07-28 and again 2026-08-08 (v3.8.0, SQLite, `source_of_truth=files`). Six stdio servers alive against one `--project-root`, oldest 12 days; one held a write transaction, so every new server's startup sync failed:

```
[2026-08-08 20:55:10] sync_rules at stdio startup failed (non-fatal): database is locked
```

Two committed rules never reached the cache — 35 rows against 37 `rules/*.md`. Searches for them returned nothing, with no error anywhere in the session. The corroborating symptom is a WAL that has not checkpointed: `knowledge.db-wal` at 2.3 MB against a 278 KB `knowledge.db`.

Widening `busy_timeout` from the hardcoded 5s (`db.py:145`) to four minutes still blocked indefinitely, so the retry path cannot recover from a genuinely held transaction — the cross-process case is not the intra-process contention fixed in #79/#83. That contention is arguably working as designed for a laptop running many sessions; the defect is that its outcome is unobservable.

Some options, roughly increasing in cost:

- Record the failure in server state and prefix affected `search` / `session_start` responses with a staleness warning, so the agent sees it at the point of use.
- Expose last-sync status (timestamp, counts, last error) as a tool or resource for explicit checks.
- Retry the startup sync in the background rather than once at boot, so a transient holder resolves itself.
- Return a non-fatal notice through the MCP client's logging channel, which is not stderr and is safe to use.

Happy to send a PR for the first if that's the direction you'd want.

# --allowed-host / MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS ignored by streamable-http transport (421 on permitted Host)

# `--allowed-host` / `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is ignored by the streamable-http transport (server 421s a permitted Host)

## Summary
When `mcm-engine serve --transport streamable-http` runs behind a reverse proxy / ingress, requests whose `Host` header is a configured allowed host are still rejected with **HTTP 421 "Invalid Host header"**. The allow-list (`--allowed-host` / `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS`) has no effect for streamable-http; only the localhost defaults (`127.0.0.1:*`, `localhost:*`, `[::1]:*`) are enforced.

## Environment
- mcm-engine 3.5.0 (also present on current `main`: `transport.py`).
- Transport: `streamable-http`, bound `--host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`.
- Reached via an internal AWS ALB at `https://mcm.internal.example` (Host = that FQDN).

## Repro
1. `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS=example.internal mcm-engine serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --transport streamable-http`
2. `curl -H 'Host: example.internal' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid>' \
   -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
   -X POST http://<addr>:8080/mcp -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}'`
3. → `421 Invalid Host header` (bearer auth passes first — an unauthenticated call 401s — so this is specifically Host validation, after auth).

Confirmed the env is read and passed: `cmd_serve` reads `MCM_ALLOWED_HOSTS` and calls `serve(..., allowed_hosts=...)`, and `_configure_transport_security` builds the expected pattern (`example.internal:*` via `_host_pattern`). Yet a live server still shows only the localhost allow-list enforcing.

## Root cause (ordering)
In `transport.py serve()`:
```python
_configure_transport_security(server, host=host, allowed_hosts=allowed_hosts, enable=...)  # mutates server.mcp.settings.transport_security
app = build_asgi_app(server, transport=transport)  # -> server.mcp.streamable_http_app()
```
`_configure_transport_security` mutates `server.mcp.settings.transport_security` **after** FastMCP is constructed, but `streamable_http_app()` builds its DNS-rebinding middleware from FastMCP's own (localhost-only) transport-security at app-build time and does not honor the post-construction mutation. So the alignment is discarded and the localhost-only list is what actually enforces. (A freshly built `MCMServer` shows `allowed_hosts=['127.0.0.1:*','localhost:*','[::1]:*']`.)

## Suggested fix
Configure FastMCP's `TransportSecuritySettings` **before** the transport app is built — e.g. construct `FastMCP` with the settings up front, or set them via whatever `streamable_http_app()` reads at build time — so `--allowed-host` takes effect for streamable-http (it may already work for `sse`; worth confirming both). Add a regression test: build the streamable-http app with an allow-list and assert a request with that Host is accepted.

## Workaround in use
Setting `MCM_DNS_REBINDING_PROTECTION=0` disables Host validation entirely and unblocks ingress access. Acceptable only on a trusted, non-browser endpoint (internal LB, private DNS) and does **not** weaken bearer auth. Not a fix — the allow-list should work.

# SessionTracker is process-global: concurrent clients corrupt each other's governance counters

## Summary

`SessionTracker` is instantiated **once per server process** and shared by every client connection. It has no notion of the MCP session id, so **concurrent clients corrupt each other's governance counters** (`turn_count`, `ignored_counts`, `calls_since`, `last_store_turn`, `last_checkpoint_turn`, `topic_freq`). Two Claude Code instances pointed at the same server — a normal, expected setup — interfere: one client's tool calls advance the nudge/escalation state that then blocks the *other* client.

## Root cause

`server.py:115`:

```python
self.tracker = SessionTracker(config.nudges)
```

Every tool handler closes over this single instance. The streamable-HTTP transport (`StreamableHTTPSessionManager`) *does* assign each client its own `mcp-session-id` at `initialize()`, but the tracker ignores it — all sessions collapse onto one counter.

## Observed impact

Running `mcm-engine ingest --remote` (which fans out into many `sift_candidates` batch calls) **while a second Claude Code session was connected to the same server** produced erratic, incomplete sift coverage: the *same* repo (`org/skills/example-skills`) surfaced 16 / 21 / 36 / 42 novel spans on successive runs, and the `import_rules` write at the end intermittently hit:

```
ESCALATED BLOCK: 'checkpoint' nudge ignored N times. You MUST call one of: save_snapshot, session_handoff before any other tool.
```

The escalation count depended on what the *other* session was doing concurrently — not on this session's own behavior. A `session_handoff` from the ingest client (to reset its gate) also blows away the other client's counters, and vice-versa.

## Expected

Each MCP session gets its own tracker state. One client's tool calls, nudges, escalations, and `session_handoff`/`reset_all` must not affect another client's governance state.

## Proposed fix

Key tracker state by `mcp-session-id`:

- Maintain a `dict[session_id, SessionTracker]` (or store per-session state in a `contextvars.ContextVar` set from the request scope), created lazily on first tool call / `initialize`, evicted on session close or TTL.
- Thread the per-request session id from the FastMCP request context down to the tool handlers (they currently receive mcm's own DB `Context`, **not** the FastMCP request `Context` that carries the session id — so this needs wiring, it isn't a one-liner).
- `session_handoff` / `save_snapshot` should reset only the calling session's tracker.

Lifecycle to decide: eviction policy (on transport session-close hook if available, else idle TTL) so long-lived servers don't leak tracker objects.

## Secondary hardening (optional, separate)

Independently of isolation, read-only tools (`sift_candidates`, `find_duplicate_rules`, `find_conflicting_rules`, `consolidation_report`, `list_rules`, `get_related`) arguably should not advance **write-hygiene** gates (`store_reminder` / `checkpoint` / `mandatory_stop`) at all — a read query is neither a mutation nor something you must checkpoint before. `sift_candidates` is the load-bearing case: even within a *single* session, one `ingest --remote` run makes enough `sift_candidates` calls to self-escalate the gate and block its own follow-up `import_rules` write. (`search` should stay counted — it resolves `rules_check` and is part of the look-first contract.) This mitigates the single-session case but does **not** substitute for per-session isolation, which is the real bug.

## Environment

- Transport: `streamable-http` under `/mcp`
- Reproduced with two Claude Code clients against one server (local kind deployment, mcm-engine at the `3.5.0` image tag).

# search blocks ~20s on SQLite lock from post-search counter bumps

# `search` blocks ~20 seconds on SQLite lock from post-search counter bumps

**Version:** 2.0.0

I've started working this into my homelab setup piece (project) by piece. I think I've hit a performance issue and wanted to share what I found in case it's useful.

## Symptom

Every `search` call takes ~15–30 seconds; longer queries exceed a 30 sec. client timeout and return nothing. Reproduces on a single idle `mcm-engine run` (stdio) against its own copy of a small (27-rule) tree with no external concurrency. Timing is deterministic (~20.9 s for the same 3-term query), so it doesn't look like network or model-load.

## What I found

The search itself is fine; the stall is a SQLite lock wait, not work:

- `sample <pid>` mid-call is 100% in `sqlite3_step → unixSleep → nanosleep` (the `busy_timeout` back-off).
- Calling the read-only adapter directly: `SqliteSearch.search(...)` returns in **0.4 ms**.
- The time is in the post-search `hit_count` / `last_hit_at` bumps in `_scope_block` (tools/search.py:243-254) — up to ~2 writes × limit × 2 scopes per call.
- Those writes appear to self-contend across the embedded adapters' separate connections to the same file (db.py:117-132, `busy_timeout=5000`). Reproduced in isolation: two connections / one file, second writer blocks **5262 ms** then `database is locked`. A few of those per search ≈ the ~20 s observed.

The `try/except` around `counters.increment` (search.py:248-253) swallows the resulting exception so results still return, but the 5 s sleep happens before the exception is raised.

## Possible directions (whatever fits best)

1. Lower `busy_timeout` (e.g. ~250 ms) for the bump path. This bounds the worst case to ~1 s.
2. Run the best-effort bumps on the same connection that served the read, or off the request path.
3. A single shared writer connection for the embedded adapters.

Happy to open a PR or provide more detail (sample output, repro script) if that would help.

prompts.spec:
# Rule-like gate rejects descriptive architectural facts (normative-word requirement too strict for ingest)

## Summary

`is_rule_like` (`src/mcm_engine/ingest/rulesift.py`) requires a **normative/warning marker** (`must|never|always|avoid|ensure|require|note|warning|gotcha|…`) for a span to survive the funnel. This drops **descriptive architectural facts** that are genuinely rule-worthy knowledge but phrased declaratively rather than as an imperative.

## Repro

Ingesting `DoddE/stork` (a real Terraform artifact-repository project) via `ingest --remote`:

```
# funnel:   19 raw candidates -> 0 rule-like span(s)
```

All 19 candidates were dropped. The README describes a real "dirty/clean" artifact-promotion architecture (AWS CodeArtifact intake→scan→clean, Harbor+Trivy, EventBridge-triggered promotion, internal ALB) — high-value KB content — but contains no `must`/`never`/`note`/`gotcha`, so `is_rule_like` returns `False` for every span.

## Root cause

`is_rule_like` (rulesift.py:140):

```python
def is_rule_like(text: str) -> bool:
    if len(dedup.normalize(text).split()) < MIN_TOKENS:
        return False
    return _NORMATIVE_RE.search(text) is not None   # <-- requires a normative marker
```

`_NORMATIVE_RE` is deliberately tight (comment: "over-admitting here just means more spans reach the future model stage, but for Slice 1 the agent eyeballs survivors, so we keep the gate tight").

Note this gate runs in **two** places and both must agree:
- client-side in `extract`/funnel (`sift`)
- **server-side** in `sift_spans` (rulesift.py) behind the `sift_candidates` MCP tool

So a client can't bypass it alone — `sift_candidates` re-applies `is_rule_like`.

## Impact

Now that there's a curation/adjudication stage downstream (e.g. an LLM adjudicator deciding keep/skip on survivors — see the platform's `gitlab_ingest.py` flow), the tight normative gate is the wrong place to enforce precision. It silently discards descriptive architecture, contracts, and conventions before anything smarter can judge them. The "Slice 1 agent eyeballs survivors" assumption no longer holds for automated ingest.

## Proposed fix (options)

1. **Broaden `is_rule_like`** to admit descriptive-but-substantive spans: markdown headings + prose, "X provides/creates/uses Y" declaratives, tables, module/contract descriptions — while still dropping trivially short spans and pure API-doc boilerplate (`Args:`/`Returns:`).
2. **Add a `gate=` / `strict=` parameter** to `sift_spans` (and expose it on the `sift_candidates` tool) so callers can opt into "band everything, let the caller/adjudicator decide" while keeping MinHash novelty banding + intra-run dedup. Backward-compatible default = current strict behavior.
3. Combination: keep a *minimum-substance* floor (token count, not just `MIN_TOKENS=3`; reject nav/boilerplate) but drop the hard normative-marker requirement when `gate=False`.

Option 2 is the least disruptive and unblocks automated descriptive-content ingest without changing default behavior for existing callers.

## Acceptance

- `ingest --remote` on a descriptive repo like stork yields non-zero rule-like spans (via the new mode/broadened gate).
- Existing strict behavior remains the default (no regression for curated rule ingest).
- Both client `sift` and server `sift_spans`/`sift_candidates` honor the same setting.

prompts.spec:
# link_knowledge requires entry ids that no tool surfaces, and its escalated nudge hard-blocks discovery (deadlock)

## Summary

`link_knowledge` requires integer entry ids (`source_id`, `target_id`), but **no tool surfaces those ids** — `search` and `kb_recall` render titles + bodies, never the row id. So a caller cannot know what to pass.

This compounds into a **deadlock**: the periodic-nudge system escalates an ignored `link_knowledge` nudge into a **hard block that forbids *all* other tools — including `search`** — until `link_knowledge` is called. In that state you must call `link_knowledge` but cannot look up the ids to pass it, forcing a blind guess (which creates wrong edges — the exact opposite of what the relations graph is for) or repeated errors.

## Repro (hit live)

1. Store several knowledge entries over a session without calling `link_knowledge`.
2. The nudge escalates: every tool call is rejected with `ESCALATED BLOCK: 'periodic:link_knowledge' ... You MUST call link_knowledge before any other tool.`
3. Try to discover ids to link → `search` is also blocked.
4. Only option left: guess ids by insertion order (I guessed knowledge `12 -> 10`). Guess is unverifiable and likely wrong.

## Why it's bad

- The feature is unusable as designed: you can't build correct edges without ids you can't obtain.
- The escalation actively drives *garbage* edges (blind guesses), polluting the very graph `get_related` traverses.
- Blocking the read tool needed to satisfy the nudge is a self-defeating gate.

## Fix options (pick one or more)

1. **Surface entry ids in `search` / `kb_recall` output.** Cheapest; makes correct linking possible at all. (Probably necessary regardless of the others.)
2. **Let `link_knowledge` resolve by title/slug** in addition to integer id.
3. **Don't put id-requiring tools in the hard-block set** — keep `link_knowledge` advisory, or guarantee at least one read tool (`search`) stays usable while blocked so the nudge is satisfiable.
4. **Nudge system invariant:** never escalate-to-block a tool whose required inputs cannot be obtained from the blocked state.

## Relevant code

- `src/mcm_engine/tools/relations.py` — `link_knowledge`
- `src/mcm_engine/tools/search.py` — `search` result rendering (add ids)
- `src/mcm_engine/tracker.py` + `mcm-engine.yaml` (`nudges.periodic_tools`, `nudge_escalation_threshold`) — escalation/blocking

Found while dogfooding the mcm KB during the ingest-funnel work.

prompts.spec:
# Piece C: one-way DB→git review mirror (gap 5, reviewability)

Part of the **mcm v3 Foundation Quad** (`mcm_v3_plan.md`, Piece C). A one-way DB→git review mirror: replay the DB into a git repo of markdown for audit/review (`git blame`, diff, PR review) — never authoritative, never writes `rules_paths`.

## Design — v1 = current-state snapshot
Not per-event replay: historical bodies aren't stored per-event (only `content_hash`), so per-event commits would misrepresent blame. Enumerate via `iter_entries(EntityType.RULE)`, render with `_generate_rule_content` + `_slugify` (`tools/rules.py:97`,`:27`) to `<out>/<category>/<slug>.md`, then commit. Run periodically.

## Depends on Piece A2 (not independent)
`iter_entries` enumerates superseded rows once A2 lands. The mirror MUST filter to active (`valid_until IS NULL` / `status=active`) by default, OR mirror history under a `superseded/` subtree. Never present dead rules as authoritative markdown. **Land A before C.**

## git guards
- Explicit identity: `git -c user.email=… -c user.name=…` (a fresh container has none).
- Empty case: check for changes or `commit --allow-empty`, so a no-change run doesn't error.

## Seams
New `cmd_export_mirror` in `cli.py`, registered like `cmd_migrate`; storage via `open_storage(dsn)`; `--out <git-dir>`; shell to `git` via `subprocess` (no git dep exists).

## One-way safety
Read methods only + writes into the external git dir → structurally cannot trigger the `sync_rules` orphan-archive sweep (`tools/rules.py:743`).

## Tests (TDD, test-first)
`test_cli_ingest.py` style: mirror test (temp DB → temp git dir → files + commit + `rules_paths` untouched + DB unchanged); superseded-rule-excluded test; no-change / no-identity guard test.

Phase-2 evolution: Letta-style git-native write path (commit-per-write + per-agent lock) would also solve concurrent-write clobber.

See `mcm_v3_plan.md` for full context.

prompts.spec:
# Follow-up (#25/#26): scale-free relevance via batch min-max (fix adapter-scale mismatch)

#26's relevance sigmoid uses a fixed midpoint (~8.0) calibrated for SQLite FTS5 **bm25** (magnitudes ~1–20). The production pod is **Postgres**, whose `ts_rank_cd` scores are ~0.1–1 — so the sigmoid collapses relevance to ~0 there and counters dominate (a live ranking regression). Fix: replace the fixed-scale sigmoid with **batch min-max relative normalization** (Generative-Agents style) — normalize each result's relevance across the candidate batch's own min/max, in the search layer (two-pass). Scale-free: works for bm25, ts_rank_cd, and any future adapter with zero per-scale tuning. `compose_rank` then takes a pre-normalized `relevance ∈ [0,1]`; drop `query_terms`. TDD in test_scoring.py.
